query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Under high-temperature sliding wear, the overall wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin protective coatings is governed by the dynamic formation of an ultra‐fine grained, oxide-enriched tribolayer that reduces friction and slows material removal.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu thin film produced by standard deposition methods with a conventional (coarser) polycrystalline microstructure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a microstructural refinement step—such as ultrasonic vibration-assisted deposition or a controlled post-deposition annealing—to yield a finer initial grain structure in the coating.
generation.conditions: Wear testing performed in air at elevated temperatures (approximately 600–800°C) under representative high contact loads.
generation.structural_mediator: A dynamic, ultra-nanocrystalline and oxide-rich near-surface tribolayer generated during sliding contact at high temperatures.
generation.mechanism: At high temperature, sliding contact induces rapid localized oxidation and deformation-induced grain refinement. A more refined initial microstructure enhances the formation and uniformity of a protective oxide-rich layer, lowering friction and wear rates by impeding further material removal.
generation.predicted_outcome: The refined coatings will exhibit more uniform and adherent nano/oxide tribolayers on the worn surfaces, accompanied by lower friction coefficients and reduced wear volumes compared to the baseline (coarser-grained) coatings.
generation.baseline: Standard as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin coating with a coarser grain structure and without the additional microstructural refinement intervention.
generation.boundary: The mechanism is expected to be effective within high-temperature regimes (600–800°C) under significant sliding loads; its contribution may be less pronounced at lower temperatures where oxidation and dynamic grain refinement are minimal.
generation.uncertainty: It remains unclear to what extent the oxidation versus the grain refinement independently contributes to the observed wear resistance; quantitative differences in friction reduction and wear rate improvement are also not precisely predicted.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin coatings on the same conventional metal substrate: one using the standard deposition process (baseline) and the other incorporating a microstructural refinement step (e.g., ultrasonic vibration-assisted deposition). Subject both sets to sliding wear tests in air at 600–800°C under identical high-load conditions. Post-test, employ SEM/TEM and XPS to characterize the near-surface tribolayer and measure friction coefficients and wear volume losses.
measurements: Coefficient of friction during wear tests
Microstructural analysis of worn surfaces (grain size, oxide content, layer uniformity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the refined coatings do not develop a more uniform ultra-fine, oxide-rich tribolayer or if friction coefficients and wear volume losses do not show statistically significant improvement compared to the baseline coatings under high-temperature conditions, the hypothesis would be falsified.

Design and Effect of Resonant Ultrasonic Vibration-Assisted Laser Cladding (R-UVALC) on AlCrFeMnNi High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: The design of the resonant ultrasonic vibration-assisted laser cladding (R-UVALC) setup involved employing finite element analysis (FEA) to simulate the ultrasonic transducer, horn, and workpiece in a resonance state. The impact of R-UVALC on AlCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloys was assessed using various ultrasonic vibration amplitudes of 0, 5, 10, and 15 µm, with a constant frequency of 20 kHz. Ultrasonic vibrations reduced pores and cracks and increased the clad breadth, melt pool wetting angle, and laser-clad layer consistency. The columnar elongated grains in proximity to the substrate surface underwent a size reduction and transformed into grains with a more equiaxed shape with the utilization of ultrasonic vibrations at an amplitude of 5 µm. Laser cladding performed without ultrasonic vibrations yields two phases: face-centered cubic (FCC) and body-centered cubic (BCC). Microstructural Evolution of AlCoCrFeNiSi High-Entropy Alloy Powder during Mechanical Alloying and Its Coating Performance

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are promising structural materials due to their excellent comprehensive performances. The use of mechanically alloyed powders to deposit HEA coatings through atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) is an effective approach that can broaden the application areas of the HEAs. In this paper, a ductility–brittleness AlCoCrFeNiSi system was chosen as an object of study, and the detailed evolution of the surface morphology, particle size distribution, and microstructure of the powder during mechanical alloying was investigated. An AlCoCrFeNiSi HEA coating was deposited using powder milled for 10 h, which can be used as an ideal feedstock for APS. The surface morphology, microstructure, microhardness, and wear behavior of the coating at room temperature were investigated. The results showed that as the milling time increased, the particle size first increased, and then decreased. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2).
